# Preface {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning}
**Draft 0.6.** This is an early draft, written with substantial help from a large language model working from an outline, source-literature notes, and detailed comments by the author. Everything in it is provisional, and a further chapter on measurement is not written yet. The git history records what was written by the author and what was generated.
:::

Most statistics courses teach methods one at a time: here is the *t*-test, here is regression, here is ANOVA. You leave with a well-stocked toolbox and no manual. Which tool answers which question, and when should anyone believe the answer? This book starts from the other end. Every empirical study, from a survey to a transformer, follows the same basic logic:

> A **research question** motivates a **design** for collecting data; the design makes a set of **assumptions** plausible; those assumptions are the **model**; and the results of fitting the model answer the question, to the extent that the assumptions hold.

The chapters work through this logic. First the logic itself (@sec-rq-to-interpretation). Then, concretely, how to build a statistical model out of a theory stated in words (@sec-theory-to-glm), and what happens when the design cannot answer the question at all (@sec-identification). Then a supposedly old-fashioned idea, the analysis of variance, is rehabilitated as the gateway to multilevel models and to meta-analysis (@sec-anova). A hinge chapter steps back to ask what prediction is for (@sec-explanation-prediction). The last three chapters cross into machine learning: what overfitting is and why the bias-variance tradeoff governs every model (@sec-overfitting), how to evaluate predictions honestly, from cross-validation and the bootstrap to what happens when a well-scored model meets the world (@sec-evaluation), and what happens to all of this when the outcome disappears and the task is to find groups rather than to predict (@sec-unsupervised).

Each chapter contains two kinds of exercises. Inline exercises appear throughout; do them immediately, and click to reveal the answer below each one. The "Test yourself" exercises at the end of each chapter are harder. They test whether you can use the ideas, not whether you can nod along to them.

The practical exercises use R. Everything can be done in Python too; the ideas are what matter.

The book is available as a website, as a PDF sized for printing, and as an EPUB; the download links are in the sidebar. A second PDF, with the answers to all exercises collected at the back rather than beside the questions, is at [stads-book-answers-in-back.pdf](https://daob.github.io/stads-book/stads-book-answers-in-back.pdf). Source, data-preparation scripts, and the issue tracker live at [github.com/daob/stads-book](https://github.com/daob/stads-book).
